content.p: On Sunday 30 November 1941 and again on 8 December, columns of Jews were marched out of the Riga ghetto to a stretch of pine forest beside the Rumbula railway station and shot at the edge of pits that had been dug for them. In two days, at least 25,000 people were killed, most of them Latvian Jews from the ghetto. Rumbula was planned by an SS general who had already run such shootings in Ukraine, and it was carried out with the help of Latvian auxiliary police.

The killing emptied most of the ghetto, which had been sealed only five weeks earlier. Its houses were then handed to Jews deported from Germany, Austria and Czech lands, some of whom found the meals of the dead still on the tables.
content.h2: A ghetto built to be emptied
content.p: German troops reached Riga on 1 July 1941, accompanied by elements of Einsatzgruppe A. According to the Holocaust Historical Society, the first written mention of a ghetto is dated 21 July, and in August nearly 30,000 Latvian Jews were moved by force into a working-class district known as the Moscow suburb. The decree establishing it was published on 23 October, and on 25 October it was fenced in with a double line of barbed wire guarded by men of the 20th Latvian Police Battalion.

The same source says the Germans treated the ghetto as a short-term measure, because they had already decided to kill most of Latvia's Jews. Mass shootings of male Jews by Einsatzgruppe A, helped by the Latvian auxiliary police under Viktors Arajs, had been carried out through the summer and autumn. EBSCO's research summary puts the number of Latvian Jews killed by October 1941 at about 34,000. History Hit, by contrast, says that by 15 October around 30,000 had been murdered. The figures differ by several thousand, and neither source explains how it counted.

The reason given for clearing Riga's Jews was space. According to EBSCO, the aim was to destroy the Latvian Jewish community and put deported German and Austrian Jews in the vacated homes. Wolfgang Scheffler, the German historian of the deportations, said in a 2000 lecture that when transports from the Reich began, Riga in fact had no accommodation ready, despite assurances from the Einsatzgruppe A commander, Walter Stahlecker. According to Scheffler, Jeckeln, as Higher SS and Police Leader for Ostland, then ordered the ghetto, closed only on 25 October 1941, to be cleared. The Deutsche Biographie says Himmler named him to the post on 1 November 1941.
content.h2: The man who chose the site
content.p: Friedrich Jeckeln, who grew up in the Black Forest town of Hornberg, had joined the Nazi party in 1929 and the SS the following year. The Deutsche Biographie says that in the first months of the war against the Soviet Union he bore a share of responsibility for the escalation of the shootings of Jews in Ukraine, among them the killing of 23,600 people at Kamianets-Podilskyi in three days and the massacre at Babi Yar, where an Einsatzgruppe report counted 33,771 victims. The same entry estimates that the victims of war crimes he was answerable for in Ukraine were far more than 170,000.

Within weeks of reaching Riga he organised Rumbula. A document quoted by Yahad-In Unum, an extract from the German criminal judgment against Arajs, says that Jeckeln drew up the plan on the model of the operation tested in southern Russia, and chose the site himself during a car journey. It lay a few kilometres from the ghetto, a few hundred metres off the Riga to Daugavpils road, on hilly ground with dry sandy soil. The judgment says his construction chief, SS-Untersturmführer Ernst Hemicker, was told to plan pits for 25,000 to 28,000 people, and designed six or perhaps more, each about three metres deep and ten by ten metres, with sloping ramps so that people aged 15 and over could walk in. History Hit adds that the only drawback Jeckeln saw was the nearby highway, since gunfire on the raised ground would carry for miles.

Soviet prisoners of war dug the pits. A Soviet commission deposition by the survivor Noa Heimanson, quoted by Yahad, says about 100 of those prisoners were shot afterwards so that none would remain as a witness.

In the second half of November the Germans told the ghetto that some residents would be relocated to a camp to relieve overcrowding, according to Alfred Winter, a ghetto inmate whose memoir is archived on a Rumbula remembrance website. Part of the ghetto was cut off with barbed wire along Ludzas Street. The Jews who were still working were moved into this smaller section.

On the morning of 30 November the workers left as usual. When they came back that evening, Winter wrote, nearly half the ghetto was empty. There were bodies in the streets and blood on the snow, and houses had been ransacked. German and Latvian police had gone from house to house, shooting or beating anyone who resisted or could not move quickly. Residents had been formed into columns five abreast and marched toward Salaspils, he recalled, and the majority of those left behind believed that a camp had been set up there. Winter's own guess was that close to 500 were killed in the ghetto that day. Heimanson's deposition says more than 1,000 were shot inside it.

The march to Rumbula was itself a killing ground. A passage reproduced by History Hit, without naming its author, describes columns moving "sometimes at a half run" while guards urged them on with whips and rifle butts, and the old people, pregnant women, children and disabled who fell behind were left in the road. The oral history of Steven Springfield at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum describes the same morning: Latvian and German police, in his words mostly drunk, driving everyone out, shooting those who could not walk, and German officers telling the old and the weak that buses would carry them. Springfield recalled that at the forest the victims were told to undress, sort their clothes and shoes into piles, and were driven to the pit edges and machine-gunned. He put the day's toll at 15,000.

Different sources describe the shooting in terms that do not quite agree. EBSCO's summary says victims were made to lie face down in the trench and were shot once in the back of the head, that when the pit floor filled the next group lay on top of the dead, and that anyone still alive was buried. History Hit writes that as the light faded executioners sometimes missed, and that Latvian guards were posted around the pits to shoot anyone who climbed out. It quotes the survivor Max Kaufmann: "the earth still heaved for a long time because of the many half-dead people." The Baltic Times, reporting in 2002, said victims were shot at a rate of about 1,000 per hour.

That morning, the first deportation train to arrive directly in Riga pulled in from Berlin. Scheffler writes that roughly 730 Berlin Jews who had left home on 27 November died early that day, just before the ghetto's Latvian Jews reached the forest. The Holocaust Historical Society gives the number as 1,000 and says Jeckeln decided on his own authority to kill them with the Latvian Jews. According to that account, Dr Rudolf Lange, head of the Security Police in Latvia, refused to take part in the murder of German Jews without an order from the Reich Security Main Office in Berlin and withdrew his men, so that the first day's killing was done by the German Order Police alone. The difference between 730 and 1,000 is not resolved in the pages used here, though later summaries (the Jewish Community of Latvia and the Baltic Times) settle on about 1,000 from Germany.

The second operation began after the Germans had separated young, fit workers from the rest. According to the Holocaust Historical Society, they were moved into a separate section on the evening of 7 December. Only Latvian Jews were killed this time, and the Security Police took an active part. The same page puts the second day's victims at more than 14,000, which, on that account, brought the two days to at least 25,000.

The survivor Marģers V. told Yahad that people were made to walk about ten kilometres in winter, and that behind the column a horse-drawn sledge used for clearing snow collected the bodies of those who fell. Winter writes that this time was "far worse" than the first, with nearly 900 killed inside the ghetto, and that police sergeant Otto Tuchel shot some of the men clearing the corpses because they did not move fast enough. His own estimate for the second day was 12,000 to 14,000 removed, leaving about 3,000 to 4,000 young Jews alive as forced labourers.

Heimanson told the Soviet commission that on 7 and 8 December 10,000 Jews were shot, some at Rumbula and some in the Biķernieki forest. Her totals for the first day, 18,000, are far higher than the 11,000 given by the Holocaust Historical Society. Winter believed the removal on 30 November took 13,000 to 15,000, and History Hit's account of the first march speaks of almost 12,000.

The pages used here do not agree on a single total. EBSCO says about 25,000 and the Jewish Community of Latvia says more than 25,000. The Deutsche Biographie says 27,500 people from the ghetto were shot on 30 November and 8 and 9 December, while Scheffler gives 26,500 Latvian Jews murdered by SS, police and Latvian auxiliaries. The Baltic Times, reporting the 2002 unveiling, gives 26,000, of whom 25,000 were from Latvia and 1,000 from Germany, while the BBC's report of the same event says 25,000. Winter, looking back, thought that 28,000 to 30,000 had died in the two operations. By February 1942, History Hit says, about 3,500 Latvian Jews remained.

In an interrogation dated 14 December 1945 and reproduced in an Einsatzgruppen archive, Jeckeln stated that he took part in the shootings on three occasions, as did Lange and other officials. He said all the Jews walked from the ghetto, left their outer clothing near the pits, and that the clothes were washed, sorted and sent to Germany. He told his interrogators that he reported to Himmler by telephone that the Riga ghetto had been liquidated, then in person at Lötzen in December 1941, and that Himmler was satisfied and told him more transports would come. According to Winter, Jeckeln also said at his trial that Latvia was the right place because anti-Semitism there was so strong that Latvian helpers needed no persuading. That is Winter's report of the statement, not a quotation from a court record that the pages show.
Jeckeln was tried by a Soviet military tribunal in Riga. The Deutsche Biographie records that he was sentenced to death on 3 February 1946 and hanged publicly the same day.

The emptied houses were filled quickly. The Holocaust Historical Society says about 22,000 German, Austrian and Czech Jews arrived between the late autumn of 1941 and mid-1942. Winter described one group arriving on 15 December and finding frozen food on tables, bloodstained clothes on floors and baby carriages with bottles of frozen milk in the snow, until a woman who crossed the street was shot by a Latvian guard and the truth sank in.
Several hundred Jewish men from the Kaiserwald concentration camp were killed at the same site in 1944, according to the Jewish Community of Latvia.

The question of who else was held to account is answered in part by Scheffler: Stahlecker died in 1942 and Lange in 1945, while Arajs lived undetected in West Germany for years before a Hamburg court sentenced him to life imprisonment in 1979.

For years after the war the killing site went unmarked. The Jewish Community of Latvia says that in 1964, after a long struggle with the Soviet authorities, local Jewish activists obtained a memorial stone reading "To the Victims of Fascism" in Latvian, Russian and Yiddish. A wooden plaque and a poster by the artist Josif Kuzkovskis, put up in 1963, were removed in 1964, according to the Military Heritage Tourism site.

The present memorial was opened on 29 November 2002, with funding from institutions in Latvia, Israel, the United States and Germany. It has a menorah above a Star of David, stones bearing victims' names, ghetto street names cut into the paving and the six mass graves marked with concrete borders. At the unveiling, President Vaira Vike-Freiberga said: "It is a sad and black day in the history of Latvia", and the BBC reported that it was the first monument in the country to acknowledge the involvement of the local population. The Baltic Times quoted US ambassador Brian Carlson saying that of 1,700 people who took part in the killings, between 1,000 and 1,500 were Latvian residents. Prime Minister Einars Repse said that unpleasant facts could not be changed or hidden. According to the Baltic Times, City Council members had debated fiercely beforehand how far the plaque should acknowledge Latvian culpability.
